questions.q: What does Waldfogel call the pre-internet system where industry insiders picked and funded artists?
a: The adult supervision model
The gatekeeper economy
The star factory system
The patronage model
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes talent scouts and their employers investing heavily in chosen artists, which he calls adult supervision.

questions.q: What does the saying that nobody knows anything about art actually mean?
a: Taste is subjective and hard to predict, even for experts
Critics understand art better than audiences do
Only trained artists can judge quality
Nobody can agree on what counts as art
questions.why: Lesson 1 says even seasoned professionals misjudge hits, as with the costly flop Solo: A Star Wars Story.

questions.q: What happened to creative industry jobs and output after digitization?
a: Jobs and revenue fell while available art soared
Both jobs and the amount of art declined sharply
Jobs grew steadily along with artistic output
Revenue rose but the number of new works dropped
questions.why: Lesson 2 notes movie jobs and earnings dropped, yet the art reaching consumers increased enormously.

questions.q: What was copyright protection originally meant to do?
a: Let creators recoup costs and profit from their work
Keep all art under the control of publishers
Prevent artists from selling abroad
Guarantee every creator a steady income
questions.why: Lesson 3 says copyright existed so artists could earn from their work and keep making more.

questions.q: Why does the summary argue that stricter copyright enforcement is pointless now?
a: Artists keep creating despite widespread file sharing
Piracy has been almost completely eliminated
Consumers refuse to pay for any digital art
Governments have already repealed copyright laws
questions.why: Lesson 3 observes that artistic production continues at full steam even though copyright is widely ignored.
